extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, and ornithologists (readers of Darwinian theory and sexual selection)
extracted.subtask_description: Defines classes and explanatory principles for relationships among adult male, adult female, and young plumages (sex-, age-, and season-limited transmission), and discusses causes such as sexual selection, natural selection for protection, and the timing of variation. Useful for categorizing species and inferring evolutionary mechanisms for plumage differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: CLASS III — WHEN THE ADULT MALE RESEMBLES THE ADULT FEMALE, THE YOUNG OF BOTH SEXES HAVE A PECULIAR FIRST PLUMAGE OF THEIR OWN.
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where adult sexes resemble each other, but the young of both sexes have a distinctive first plumage different from adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: male robin and female similar while young are mottled; scarlet ibis adults alike but young brown. Explanation: bright adult colours probably acquired through sexual selection by nearly mature males and then transmitted to both sexes (transmission limited to same age, not same sex). Discussion includes uncertainty whether the successive variations first appeared in males when nearly mature or while young; either way sexual selection acted when males competed for females; inheritance at corresponding ages may later transfer characters to the young. Observations of anomalous young assuming adult plumage are noted (e.g., Lanius rufus, Colymbus glacialis).

rubrics_metrics.name: CLASS IV — WHEN THE ADULT MALE RESEMBLES THE ADULT FEMALE, THE YOUNG OF BOTH SEXES IN THEIR FIRST PLUMAGE RESEMBLE THE ADULTS.
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where adults of both sexes and the young closely resemble one another in plumage (though similarity is rarely complete).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: kingfisher, some woodpeckers, jay, magpie, crow, hedge-warbler. The young are generally less vividly coloured and may retain vestiges of former plumage (e.g., feather edges). Similarity often 'graduates away' into dissimilarity. Probable cause: males acquired ornamentation by sexual selection and transmitted colours equally (or nearly equally) to offspring of both sexes; whether variations arose early or late in life is uncertain, but transmission to both sexes occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: CLASS V — WHEN THE ADULTS OF BOTH SEXES HAVE A DISTINCT WINTER AND SUMMER PLUMAGE, WHETHER OR NOT THE MALE DIFFERS FROM THE FEMALE, THE YOUNG RESEMBLE THE ADULTS OF BOTH SEXES IN THEIR WINTER DRESS, OR MUCH MORE RARELY IN THEIR SUMMER DRESS, OR THEY RESEMBLE THE FEMALES ALONE. OR THE YOUNG MAY HAVE AN INTERMEDIATE CHARACTER; OR, AGAIN, THEY MAY DIFFER GREATLY FROM THE ADULTS IN BOTH THEIR SEASONAL PLUMAGES.
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex cases in which adults have distinct seasonal (summer/winter) plumages; young may resemble adults in winter, in summer, the females, be intermediate, or differ greatly from both adult seasonal plumages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These depend on inheritance limited in three ways: by sex, by age, and by season. Examples: some egrets where young and adults are white in winter but adults become golden-buff in summer; Anastomus oscitans with reversed colours; razor-bill young resembling adult summer plumage; young white-crowned sparrows showing summer marks at fledging. Explanatory suggestions: summer (nuptial) plumage likely due to sexual selection, winter plumage possibly retained ancient state or shaped by direct conditions of life (though Darwin is skeptical). Characters acquired by adult males may be variously limited in their transmission according to age, season, and sex, producing the observed diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: CLASS VI — THE YOUNG IN THEIR FIRST PLUMAGE DIFFER FROM EACH OTHER ACCORDING TO SEX; THE YOUNG MALES RESEMBLING MORE OR LESS CLOSELY THE ADULT MALES, AND THE YOUNG FEMALES MORE OR LESS CLOSELY THE ADULT FEMALES.
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where nestlings/juveniles are sexually dimorphic from the first, with young males resembling adult males and young females resembling adult females.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: blackcap (nestlings distinguishable by head colour), blackbird (male distinguishable in nest), certain thrushes and humming-birds (Aithurus polytmus, Eustephanus) where young of each sex assume sex-typical colours early. Probable mechanism: males transmitted their colours to male offspring at earlier ages than usual; difficulty remains in understanding how both sexes of a species could independently become ornamented by sexual selection simultaneously, though shifts in sex ratios over time may explain such patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance at corresponding ages (law of inheritance at corresponding ages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offspring tend to inherit characters at the same corresponding ages at which they first appear in the parents; failures of this law can cause characters to appear earlier in offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain why young sometimes show adult characters earlier than when they first appeared in parents (e.g., some young swans born white; anomalous young assuming adult plumage). This law helps infer whether variations first appeared early or late in the life of ancestors, and thus whether transmission is sex-limited or age-limited. Darwin cites examples and notes that the law is not absolute but a useful determinant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period of variation (age when variation appears) as determinant of transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: The age at which variations first occur (early vs late in life) is an important factor determining whether the trait is transmitted to one sex only or to both sexes/ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two heuristics often referred to: variations occurring late in life are transmitted to one sex (often males only), whereas variations occurring early in life tend to be transmitted to both sexes. Darwin notes these rules apply in many cases (first, second, fourth classes) but fail in class three, often in five and six. Examples given of species requiring multiple years to attain full plumage support this principle. The period of moulting and life-duration complicate judging earliness/lateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexually-limited transmission (law of transmission limited by sex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when natural selection would equally favour protective coloration in both sexes, transmission of ornamental characters may be restricted to one sex by hereditary laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Sahara desert birds: upper surfaces of both sexes are sand-coloured (natural selection for protection), but in some species males show ornamentation on lower surfaces; yet females are not prevented by natural selection from inheriting male colours, so the explanation lies in sexually-limited transmission. Darwin emphasizes that sexually-limited inheritance must be invoked where both sexes are equally protected yet do not both display ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing causes: sexual selection (ornament) versus natural selection (protection) and direct action of conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether plumage traits arose via sexual selection for attraction, natural selection for protection (camouflage), or direct action of environmental conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines and examples: bright colours are rarely protective (parrots show ornamentation despite tree habitat); green tint in tree-haunting birds may arise by protection as an added advantage; ground birds (partridges, snipes, plovers) commonly have cryptic colours by natural selection; desert fauna often 'isabelline' sand-colour. Both processes can act conjointly (e.g., protective upper surfaces with ornamented concealed lower surfaces). Darwin is skeptical of attributing wide seasonal differences solely to direct environmental action, favouring inheritance and sexual selection explanations unless protective utility is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral/sex-ratio influences on which sex becomes ornamented (role reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral traits and relative abundance of the sexes can reverse the usual pattern of sexual selection, causing females rather than males to acquire ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites cases (Turnix, emu, peahen, wild turkey, certain grouse) where females are more pugnacious, larger, or more numerous and thus may court males; sexual selection then operates on females, producing female ornamentation while males and young remain little modified. Operational sex ratios and courtship behavior should be considered when inferring cause of ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age/season/moult timing complicates assessment of 'earliness' of variation
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging whether variation is early or late in life, different standards (absolute age, age relative to lifespan, age relative to reproductive maturity, number/timing of moults) can give conflicting impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin warns that accelerated moulting can make adult plumage appear earlier; some birds breed while in immature plumage, confounding inferences about sexual selection's role. Observers should account for species-specific moult schedules, life-span data (often unknown), and instances of breeding before full adult plumage when applying age-based transmission rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concomitant development vs continuous growth (interpretation of progressive ornament development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressive increases in ornamentation (e.g., peacock train or birds-of-paradise plumes) may result either from selection of successive beneficial variations or from continuous growth processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes uncertainty whether prolonged development of plumes is due to sexual selection of successive variations (likely for birds-of-paradise) or merely continuous growth (analogy with fishes continuing to grow). Use caution attributing long-term elaboration to sequential selection without additional evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite explanations and reluctance to over-assign causes
rubrics_metrics.description: In ambiguous cases where neither protection nor sexual selection provide clear explanations, acknowledge ignorance or attribute to direct environmental action only with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin recommends, when evidence is equivocal (e.g., soft-billed reed birds obscurely coloured), to admit lack of knowledge rather than force a conclusion. He stresses careful weighing of evidence and consideration of multiple interacting processes (sexual selection, natural selection, inheritance patterns).
